content: For children, the recommended ratio of blood to broth for culture is 1–3 mL of blood to 20 mL of broth. For adults, the ratio is 5–10 mL of blood to 50 mL of broth. Specimens should ideally be collected before the administration of antibiotics. However, the collection process should not delay the initiation of antibiotic therapy. The laboratory must be informed in advance to ensure the specimen is processed promptly. Blood and pleural fluid should be inoculated into blood culture bottles within one minute of collection and transported to the microbiology laboratory as quickly as possible for overnight incubation and bacterial growth. All inoculated blood culture media must be protected from extreme temperatures (<18°C or >37°C) using a transport carrier and thermal insulator, such as extruded polystyrene foam. Blood culture bottles should not be refrigerated. Blood should not be transported in syringes, as they lack anticoagulants, leading to coagulation within minutes. For long-term storage, isolates should preferably be stored at -70°C. If further testing (e.g., serotyping or antimicrobial susceptibility) is required, or if the local hospital lacks culture capacity, isolates can be frozen at -20°C and sent to a reference laboratory for processing. Approximately 20–40 mL of aspirated pleural fluid should be immediately placed into tubes coated with the appropriate anticoagulant (e.g., EDTA or heparin) for various tests: 5 mL for biochemistry, 5–10 mL for microbiology, 10–25 mL for cytology, and 200 μL–1 mL for PCR testing. A heparin-coated syringe must be used to measure pH. Specimens should ideally be collected before antibiotics are administered, but this should not delay treatment. The laboratory must be informed in advance to ensure timely processing. Pleural fluid should be inoculated into blood culture bottles within one minute and transported to the microbiology laboratory promptly for overnight incubation and bacterial growth. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) samples should be cultured on blood agar plates (BAP) and supplemented chocolate agar plates prepared with 5–10% sheep or horse blood. BAP is optimal for pneumococcus growth, while chocolate agar is ideal for Haemophilus influenzae. For maximum yield, all negative cultures from probable invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) cases should be subcultured after five days of incubation before being discarded. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is recommended for all suspected cases, as bacterial culture may be inhibited if antibiotics have already been administered. If PCR capacity is unavailable locally, residual volumes of the original, non-manipulated CSF can be frozen and sent to a national or regional reference laboratory for further testing. Rapid diagnostic test kits (RDTs) can quickly identify the three primary pathogens causing bacterial meningitis. However, RDTs generally identify only the species, not the serotype or serogroup. Latex agglutination testing (LAT) should be performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions, ensuring quality control. LAT kits often have a short shelf life, so expired kits must not be used. The BinaxNOW kit can detect and partially characterize pneumococcus in CSF and pleural fluid but does not identify Haemophilus influenzae. Gram staining is a reliable and cost-effective method if staff are well-trained and reagents are of high quality. On Gram stain, Streptococcus pneumoniae appears as Gram-positive, lance-shaped diplococci, sometimes in short chains, either intracellularly or extracellularly. Neisseria meningitidis appears as Gram-negative, bean-shaped diplococci. Haemophilus influenzae appears as small, pleomorphic Gram-negative rods or coccobacilli in random arrangements. Blood culture is a diagnostic tool for pneumococcal meningitis, pneumonia, and sepsis. However, its sensitivity for pneumococcal pneumonia is lower than for other syndromes, as only 10–15% of cases are bacteremic. To maximize isolate yield, all negative cultures must be subcultured after five days of incubation before being discarded. PCR and RDTs are not routinely used to detect pneumococcus or Haemophilus influenzae due to low sensitivity and specificity. All RDT results must be reported within one to two hours of testing. CSF and blood culture results must be reported to clinicians daily if performed in the hospital laboratory. The presence of microbes on Gram staining or culture of pleural fluid indicates pleural infection, but these methods have a poor yield (<50% in most studies). The absence of microbes does not exclude infection. PCR for RNA gene amplification and detection in pleural fluid samples has shown inconsistent results. All confirmed cases should have their serogroup designated to guide vaccination efforts and understand local epidemiology. Serogrouping can be performed on bacterial isolates (if available from culture) or PCR-positive clinical specimens. Specimens or isolates from confirmed or probable cases should be stored for further strain characterization. Strain characterization or whole genome sequencing (WGS) should be conducted at national, regional, or global reference laboratories, such as WHO collaborating centers for meningococcal meningitis. The Global Invasive Bacterial Vaccine-Preventable Diseases Laboratory Network, coordinated by WHO and Public Health England, supports surveillance for invasive bacterial diseases, including IMD. The network has standardized laboratory procedures, data collection guidelines, and quality assurance systems. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) testing should be performed to monitor emerging resistance during outbreaks and sporadic cases, based on laboratory capacity. The choice of antimicrobials for AMR testing should align with those used for IMD treatment and chemoprophylaxis per national or regional guidelines. If WGS is performed, AMR-related genes should be characterized. National and regional reference laboratories and WHO collaborating centers can assist with gene characterization. Sites should perform antimicrobial sensitivity testing for all Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae isolates, evaluating results by antibiotic type, route, time between antibiotic administration and culture, fluid volume cultured, geographical area, and serotype. Recommended methods include disk diffusion (modified Kirby–Bauer technique) and antimicrobial gradient strip diffusion. Pneumococcus should be tested for susceptibility to penicillins, sulfonamides, trimethoprim, and third-generation cephalosporins. Close contacts of invasive meningococcal disease (IMD) cases are at increased risk of disease. Close contacts include household members, those in the same childcare or preschool setting, long-flight travel contacts, and anyone directly exposed to respiratory or oral secretions of a case within seven days before disease onset. Vaccination and chemoprophylaxis of close contacts should follow national guidelines. Chemoprophylaxis with antibiotics should be administered as soon as possible, preferably within 24 hours of identifying the index case, as most secondary disease occurs within 72 hours of the index case’s presentation. Specific antibiotics that clear pharyngeal carriage of meningococci are recommended for chemoprophylaxis. Contact tracing is not routinely performed for pneumococcal or Haemophilus influenzae surveillance. Laboratory diagnosis is crucial for distinguishing between these diseases. All cases should be hospitalized and promptly treated with presumptive antibiotics administered parenterally (intravenously or intramuscularly). Supportive care, including fluids, oxygen, and possibly mechanical ventilation, may be necessary. Blood and CSF samples should be collected before initiating antibiotic treatment, if possible. However, treatment should not be delayed until laboratory results are available. All cases of invasive bacterial vaccine-preventable diseases (IB-VPD) should be treated promptly with appropriate antibiotics and isolation procedures, following national treatment protocols.
